items.summary: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
items.title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space

items.summary: Dynamic graph learning models how entities and their relations evolve from historical observations to predict future graph states. Existing methods do not fully address dynamic graph world modelling, which requires learning transitions from temporal context to future latent graph states. This is difficult for three reasons: nodes and relations rely on different historical evidence, structural evolution is path-dependent, and future snapshots provide sparse and realization-specific targets. We propose Dynamic Graph World Modelling (DyG-WM), the first framework to jointly predict future node and relation representations from temporal context by answering three questions: what has evolved, how it evolved, and what will evolve next. To capture what has evolved, a historical node-relation context encoder summarizes node-neighborhood trajectories and pair-specific histories. To characterize how it evolved, a node-relation path-signature encoder captures ordered structural changes. To predict what will evolve next, a dual-level joint-embedding objective predicts target-snapshot node and relation representations without reconstructing the raw graph. Experiments on 12 link-prediction and two node-classification datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DyG-WM across both tasks.
items.title: Dynamic Graph World Modelling: Learning Future Dynamics from Temporal Context

items.summary: Learning intrinsic dynamics---the relationship between actions and their consequences---is essential for world models. However, visual variations unrelated to the underlying control process can obscure this relationship in learned representations. We investigate the connection between action predictability, defined as the ability to reconstruct an action from consecutive latent states, and the preservation of intrinsic dynamics. Our central hypothesis is that encouraging action predictability discourages representations from discarding the distinctions between different actions and their consequences. We provide two complementary forms of evidence for this connection. Theoretically, we derive a positive lower bound on squared inverse prediction error when the encoder merges distinguishable outcomes of different actions from the same state and appearance, and show that forward prediction can still be exact on those transitions. Empirically, controlled appearance-diversity comparisons, supervision interventions, and latent probes support the role of action prediction in preserving control-relevant transition information. We instantiate action predictability with Concat IDM, which predicts actions from concatenated latent states and updates the shared encoder using action labels already available in offline trajectories, without changing the test-time planner. Across three independent training runs on Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM increases planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; its paired improvement is 52.9 percentage points larger than that observed with a single appearance. Together, these findings support action predictability as an inductive bias toward intrinsic dynamics and demonstrate the practical benefits of Concat IDM for latent planning under visual diversity.
items.title: Learning Intrinsic Dynamics in Latent World Models

items.summary: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/
items.title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling

items.summary: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.
items.title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models

items.summary: Python code that reproduces all results, figures and supporting tables of Dixit, AchutaRao and Sandeep, "Future Warming Shortens the Memory of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and Erodes a Source of Near-Term Predictability" (submitted to Earth's Future). The analysis uses eleven CMIP6 models (piControl, historical, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5), the CESM2 and MIROC6 large ensembles and ERSSTv5, regridded to the 2-degree ERSSTv5 grid. "bash run_all.sh" runs the full analysis. The folder results/ contains the outputs used in the paper, from which most figures can be redrawn without the model data. See README.md for requirements, input data layout and the mapping of scripts to sections, figures and tables.
items.title: Code and results for "Future Warming Shortens the Memory of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and Erodes a Source of Near-Term Predictability"

items.summary: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.
items.title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models

items.summary: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.
items.title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation?

items.summary: EHR2Trace converts local hospital EHR extracts (delimited text and spreadsheets) into OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS. The two targets are derived independently from a single canonical layer rather than one from the other, every published row carries a link back to the source rows it came from, and fifty-five checks encode the properties a conversion must satisfy before it can be used as training data, including the leakage failures that are invisible to schema validation. Where the data does not answer a question, the converter blocks and says so instead of substituting a default. Companion paper: EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents (arXiv:2609.38193).
items.title: EHR2Trace: a deterministic converter from local EHR exports to OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS, with row-level lineage

items.summary: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.
items.title: Depth Memory

items.summary: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
items.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models

items.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

items.summary: World action models (WAMs) predict actions and future observations, typically from a reconstruction-based representation that carries noisy, redundant information which can complicate downstream predictions. We introduce LeWAM, a bidirectional transformer for forward, backward, inverse dynamics and policy prediction, on a decoder-free JEPA latent trained end-to-end through all four modes. We see the following benefits: 1) Alignment: linear probes read robot and object state from LeWAM's latent better than from a regular Le World Model (a forward-only JEPA world model), while the latent ignores visual distractors as well as LeWM does and far better than a reconstruction-based WAM. 2) Acting: Closed-loop evaluations of LeWAM match a regular flow-matching policy trained on the same encoder at matched size, while also providing a world model. 3) Planning: Sampling raw actions when planning with WAMs lets MPC exploit dynamics-model inaccuracies; planning in the noise space of the policy head instead improves the closed-loop performance of these WAMs.
items.title: LeWAM: A JEPA World Action Model with Diffusion-Steering-Based MPC

items.summary: This paper develops a new predefined-time integral reinforcement learning framework for optimal control of unknown nonlinear systems. The unknown drift is first approximated by a radial basis function (RBF) neural network, together with a data-driven online identification law for updating the corresponding neural weights. After the identifier converges to a sufficiently small neighborhood of the true dynamics, the learned model is incorporated into the integral reinforcement learning (IRL) problem. Unlike conventional reinforcement-learning-based optimal control, the desired convergence time is introduced directly into the control objective: a Lyapunov function and its prescribed decay behavior are specified by the designer, and inverse-optimal control is then used to construct a compatible running cost whose optimal policy inherits the predefined-time stabilization property. The value function is approximated by a second RBF neural network, and a new critic update law is developed to impose predefined-time convergence on the critic weights. Finite informative learning data are stored in a replay buffer and reused during the critic update, thereby avoiding the need for persistent excitation throughout the closed-loop operation. Theoretical analysis proves that the critic-weight error enters a prescribed residual set within the allocated learning horizon, while the closed-loop state reaches a small neighborhood of the origin within the overall designer-specified deadline. Numerical simulations on an unknown nonlinear system verify accurate drift reconstruction, predefined-time critic learning, and closed-loop convergence.
items.title: Predefined-Time Integral Reinforcement Learning for Unknown Nonlinear Systems via Inverse-Optimal Design

items.summary: We study the relation between equal-weight circle quadrature, Gauss--Chebyshev quadrature, and planar Minkowski reconstruction. The regular $N$-point grid is an $\mathbb S^1$-design of strength $N-1$; a half-step rotation of the $2M$-point grid projects to the classical $M$-point Gauss--Chebyshev rule. A common family of quadrature-error functionals gives exact identities for integration error, mixed-area error, and support-function error. For $N\ge3$, the centered Minkowski polygon $P_N$ with perimeter $2π$ has the exact Hausdorff distance from the unit disk $B^2$ \[ d_H(P_N,B^2)=1-\fracπ{N}\cot\fracπ{N} =\frac{π^2}{3N^2}+O(N^{-4}). \] With Steiner centering, we obtain $d_H(K_μ,K_ν)\leπW_1(μ,ν)$ for balanced, nondegenerate probability measures, where $W_1$ uses geodesic distance. Its exponent is sharp even for smooth positive densities near the uniform measure. The identity $W_1(ν_N,σ)=π/(2N)$ yields a general $O(N^{-1})$ bound for the regular grid. The sharper $O(N^{-2})$ rate follows from the sparse discrepancy spectrum and the inverse multiplier $(1-k^2)^{-1}$. Finally, a perturbation estimate gives sufficient conditions for preserving the quadratic rate and its leading constant.
items.title: Gauss--Chebyshev Quadrature, $\mathbb S^1$-Designs, and the Planar Minkowski Inverse Problem: A One-Dimensional Model for Design-Induced Convex Geometry

items.summary: We establish the overarching mathematical physics framework underlying gravitational screening and electroweak mixing in Big Boot Gauge Theory (BBGT). To demonstrate that the transition from the bare gravitational constant G_bare = 6.514085763e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 (derived from CODATA 2022 constants under unit space-time momentum p = mc = 1 kg m s^-1) to the observed value G_obs = 6.67430e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 is a rigorous topological necessity rather than an arbitrary post-hoc adjustment, we formulate the screening dynamics using Möbius inversion on finite posets over the subgroup lattice of Poincaré Dodecahedral Space (S^3/I^*). We prove that non-associative transit across the e_4 Pati-Salam midpoint node acts as a Möbius topological twist, fixing the geometric inverse-square screening factor S_ZIP^-2 = (1 - 1/120)^-2 = 1.016877348. Combining this with longitudinal Z-leakage (delta_Z = 0.026892000) and non-associative midpoint transit corrections (Delta_assoc = 0.000092701) yields the exact screened laboratory constant without arbitrary tuning.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the weak mixing angle (sin^2 theta_W = 1/5 + 1/32 = 0.23125) originates from the pentagonal P_5 symmetry order of the dodecahedron combined with a 2^5 chiral energy cascade, agreeing with experiment (0.23122) to within 0.01%. Finally, we present the complete 8x8 Logical Transitive Index Matrix (T_{n->m}), showing how the 10^19 Planck-to-electroweak mass hierarchy is compressed down to a discrete compilation factor of 128.35 across the aethereal boot levels.
tags: Big Boot Gauge Theory BBGT Gravitational Screening Möbius Inversion Finite Posets Poincaré Dodecahedral Space Binary Icosahedral Group Bare Gravitational Constant CODATA 2022 Weinberg Angle Electroweak Mixing Logical Transitive Index Non-Associative Geometry ZIP-Cayley Framework Darkon Research Laboratory Quantum Gravity Hierarchy Problem
items.title: Topological Invariance of Gravitational Screening in Big Boot Gauge Theory: Möbius Poset Inversion, Pentagonal Mixing, and the T_{n->m} Transitive Hierarchy

items.summary: Code, 2.5-D finite-wavelength forward solver, datasets, trained models and result files reproducing every number in the manuscript "Source-Conditioned Neural Surrogates for Magnetotelluric Response Prediction Under Finite-Wavelength Excitation" (S. Oh). The study makes the magnetotelluric source an explicit input of a neural forward surrogate. A validated 2.5-D scattered-field solver for a source of finite along-strike wavelength generates the training data; a conditional U-Net predicts the electromagnetic fields, from which impedance and tipper are reconstructed; an aliasing ratio quantifies how much of a source perturbation a plane-wave inversion re-images as conductivity; a surrogate-domain recoverability experiment returns a source estimate close to the known synthetic value, while a direct solver re-forward shows that the recovered conductivity and wavenumber are not together a solver-consistent inverse solution; and magnetometer arrays at three geomagnetic latitudes place real settings on the dimensionless axis that the model defines. CONTENTS: README.md, LICENSE, DATA_LICENSE.txt and requirements.txt are attached unpacked. The code archive holds the analysis scripts (top level and mt3d/) and the full solver source (solver/, with the dataset generator, the Jacobian dump, the re-forward program and the unit tests); it is MIT licensed except the third-party Triangle library, which is redistributed verbatim under its own terms. The data archive holds the three datasets (dataset_dense, dataset_freq, dataset40), the trained checkpoints (ckpt/, mt3d/ckpt/), the joint-inversion and layered-earth training data (mt3d/*.npz), the plane-wave Jacobian dump (phase3/), the solver sweeps (phase1_repro/) and the result files next to the scripts that write them, all under CC BY 4.0 (DATA_LICENSE.txt). Figures and figure-drawing scripts are not included; every figure is a direct plot of a listed result file. Comments have been removed from all code written for this study. Not included: the magnetometer-array time series, which are third-party open data (EarthScope/USArray MT through the IRIS/EarthScope Data Management Center; AusLAMP Musgraves/APY through AuScope and Geoscience Australia, CC BY 4.0) and are rebuilt from those sources by the archived fetch and conversion scripts; and the field-station file that supplies the period list of the two control tests of Section S-XVII (available from the author on request).
items.title: Source-Conditioned Residual Learning for Magnetotelluric Responses Under Finite-Wavelength Excitation

items.summary: Solutions to geophysical inverse problems are generally non-unique, and greatly benefit from additional geological prior information. Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are commonly used to parametrise such information, typically restricting solutions to a lower-dimensional latent space. The final inversion result is obtained by mapping the latent space parameters to the original higher-dimensional model space using the GNNs. However, solutions then remain confined to a low-dimensional geological generative manifold; if the true Earth model lies outside of this manifold, standard latent space inversion fails. We propose a Bayesian model space inversion method that uses the generative manifold as a guide to find the solutions that lie outside this manifold. We validate our approach in non-linear travel-time tomography experiments on both simple and more geological structures. By comparing our method with model space inversion using uniform prior probabilities and standard latent-space inversion, we demonstrate that the less informative uniform prior fails to constrain the solution, while the latent space approach fails when the true Earth model lies outside of the generative manifold. Conversely, our new model-space inversion method successfully recovers complex off-manifold geological features while maintaining low solution uncertainty.
items.title: Escaping Geological Generative Prior Distributions in Bayesian Travel Time Tomography

items.summary: Centralized orchestration provides comprehensive multi-agent coordination but creates bottlenecks in scalability, adaptability, and collective performance. Decentralized approaches alleviate these bottlenecks by distributing coordination across agents, yet often leave responsibility for delegated dependencies and failure recovery unclear. To address this gap, we propose RCM, a responsibility-centered coordination mechanism that leverages commitments to couple task delegation with explicit responsibilities of the involved parties. Through recursive delegation, agents retain their upstream responsibilities while locally orchestrating downstream commitments, thereby preserving accountability across delegation chains, creating a network of local orchestration. We operationalize this mechanism locally through responsibility-constrained decision-making and a responsibility-oriented communication protocol (RCP), enabling agents to autonomously establish, manage, and terminate commitments. As agents act in parallel, their local actions continuously evolve the commitment graph, allowing global coordination to emerge and adapt toward a shared mission without centralized control. Experiments across reasoning, coding, and executable agent environments demonstrate that RCM outperforms strong centralized and decentralized coordination baselines by up to 18.7 points in task performance and 10.2 points in Responsibility, while improving failure and harm detection without task-specific training.
items.title: A Responsibility-Centered Coordination Mechanism for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Agents are increasingly interacting with other agents that act for different principals (people or organizations on whose behalf they work), such as a buyer's personal agent negotiating with an enterprise's seller agent. In such agent-to-agent (A2A) scenarios, each agent has its own environment and holds information and authority that the other cannot see. Moreover, the interests of each agent may be aligned (cooperative), partly aligned (mixed-motive), or opposed (competitive). Existing multi-agent system failure studies assume one orchestrator, shared workspace, or single principal. We ask how A2A systems fail when these assumptions are removed. We study more than 2,500 recorded runs of A2A systems built from different agent harnesses and models, spanning 488 scenarios across eight families (legal, CRM, security, commerce, etc.). From these traces, we derive $A^2$-Failures, a taxonomy of 20 A2A failure modes in four categories: (i) discovery and delegation, (ii) grounding and record consistency, (iii) verification, and (iv) conduct and fidelity. Three findings hold across every harness, model, and scenario studied: (1) discovery and interaction are driven by the phrasing of the task rather than the availability of peer agents; (2) no agent verifies a peer's factual claim on its own initiative, so an A2A system inherits the reliability of its least reliable participant unless the protocol or mechanism performs the check; and (3) the aggregate outcome score credits the agent completing the task while staying blind to the coordination, verification, and conduct failures beneath it, so A2A systems must be evaluated per agent, against each agent's own principal. We release the run logs behind the taxonomy at https://huggingface.co/datasets/a2a-salesforce/a2-failures.
items.title: Why Do Agent Teams Fail Across Boundaries? A Failure Taxonomy for Agent-to-Agent Systems with Private States

items.summary: AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC NAVIGATION AND MISSION OBSERVABILITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation Research Flagship 01 | NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli This research atlas asks a difficult engineering question: when low-Reynolds-number microfluidic flows, Brownian orientation noise, boundary adhesion, external field actuation and incomplete sensing all influence a micro/nanorobot, what would justify calling its behavior autonomous navigation rather than externally assisted motion? The volume treats navigation as an auditable, bounded mission instead of an attractive trajectory. It develops a five-layer program spanning stochastic hydrodynamics, instrument and actuation provenance, uncertainty-calibrated belief-state estimation, blinded microfluidic challenges and independent requalification. Thirty linked mathematical stations differentiate physical relations, information-theoretic functionals and proposed navigation utility measures, with assumptions, dimensions and possible falsifiers. Eighty-two research chapters each open with a core mathematical relation, followed by five independent single-page research sections. Two hundred detailed Research Gates describe decisive comparisons, confounding explanations, evidence requirements, failure conditions and successor handoff artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos offer revisionable research prototypes rather than predetermined conclusions. The key comparator is an equal-budget experiment: fixed-field sequences, microscope-assisted manual control, externally tracked predictive control and candidate fused navigation are evaluated under matched total energy, information access, geometry, time, collision limits and recovery obligations. The manuscript emphasizes blind targets, flow reversal, sensor dropouts, wall adhesion, correlated observations, full-system power accounting, censored failures and post-mission retrieval. A mission arriving at its target but leaving an unrecovered device is not counted as a fully closed success. This work is a hypothesis-generating Research Atlas v1.0, not an experimental report or a validated medical technology. External magnetic, acoustic, optical and microscope infrastructure must be disclosed; no in-vivo or clinical competence is inferred from bench-top movement. Foundational DOI-linked literature provides context, not proof of the proposed integrated system. Every major claim is designed to be revised, rejected or reconstructed by a successor team using raw evidence and pre-registered falsification rules. PARENT RESEARCH DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23046134 Original parent: NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE AT THE LIMIT. Parent-chapter lineage: Ch. 06-11 (navigation), 47-51 (estimation/control), 65 and 68 (benchmarking and transfer). The current child manuscript does not yet have an independent DOI; one would be assigned only upon actual repository deposit. Editorial release note: the manuscript prioritizes non-duplicative research content and independent testability over an artificial word-count target. It is suitable as a research architecture for additional scientific review, not a substitute for physical validation.

items.summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.
items.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems

items.summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. items.summary: AI-Assisted Social Science Research: Methods, Governance and Reason Provenance is a practical research and educational resource for documenting and governing generative-AI-assisted social-science research. The resource develops a workflow for distinguishing AI-assisted proposal generation, researcher evaluation and governance, local empirical execution, adversarial challenge, manuscript revision and reason provenance. It includes reusable templates, completed worked examples drawn from the PISA research programme, guidance on claim preservation and manuscript governance, and public-release screening materials. The resource is intended to support transparent attribution and disciplined research practice rather than to prescribe a universal workflow or to provide evidence that AI-assisted research is inherently superior to human-only research.
items.title: AI-Assisted Social Science Research: Methods, Governance and Reason Provenance

items.summary: Multi-agent collaboration has emerged as a critical paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks; however, while coordination protocols continue to advance, systemic failures at the inter-agent collaboration interface remain a pervasive bottleneck. In collaborative workflows, systems frequently suffer from \emph{broken handoffs}---where critical task context is omitted, misrouted, or ignored despite each agent emitting locally plausible responses. To address this challenge, we present \method, a verifiable runtime control framework that treats handoff repair as selective intervention over explicit dependency graphs. Central to \method is an integrated fault-attribution and calibration pipeline, \dataset, which decouples execution dependencies and injects counterfactual handoff perturbations to provide empirical supervision for runtime intervention. Leveraging this diagnostic foundation, \method dynamically compiles observable interaction traces into a provenance graph to pinpoint unresolved dependencies, without accessing private agent states. It then evaluates candidate repairs through an empirical gate that weighs expected gains against disruption risks, and executes repairs only when formal local postconditions hold. Extensive evaluations across demanding benchmarks demonstrate that \method boosts task success by up to 12.3 absolute percentage points on SILO-BENCH and 11.1 on TeamBench. Across both backbones, \method maintains strict cost-effectiveness, adding as little as 2.0\% marginal token overhead. Furthermore, on 562 handoff-relevant traces from the MAST benchmark, \method achieves 69.8\% F1 in a single pass, establishing a reliable operational boundary for verifiable coordination repair.
items.title: BRIDGE: Selective Boundary Repair with Dependency Graph Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: This record provides the public, non-confidential analytical and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript “When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? A Borehole-Aware Empirical-to-Synthetic Validation Framework for Urban Tunnelling.” The study develops and audits a borehole-aware empirical-to-synthetic framework for evaluating whether adding downhole seismic information provides defensible incremental value in predicting the Ménard pressuremeter modulus under held-out validation. The empirical benchmark comprises 41 support-matched pressuremeter–seismic records across 21 independent boreholes from the Isfahan Metro Line 2 investigation. The framework compares a reference model, a geotechnical/geological-depth baseline, a seismic-only branch, naive multimodal fusion, and a dependence-aware fusion branch using leave-one-borehole-out validation. The public release contains a de-identified 41-record benchmark dataset, final manuscript Figure 1–5 assets, the current Supplementary Material and Supplementary Figure S1, released derived analytical outputs, provenance and reproducibility documentation, reproducibility and repository-audit scripts, computational-environment specifications, and SHA-256 integrity information. The de-identified dataset replaces source borehole identifiers with pseudonymous identifiers and excludes borehole coordinates and other spatially identifying source information. The underlying Isfahan Metro Line 2 geotechnical, geophysical, and pressuremeter source records are controlled by the Isfahan Urban Railway Organization and are not publicly redistributable. Original source workbooks, proprietary project documents, spatially identifying information, and other restricted source-derived materials are intentionally excluded from this public archive. Permission was obtained to use and publish the de-identified, non-confidential data extracted from the project report and the derived analytical information included in this release. The public code component provides scripts for reproducing the released manuscript-level benchmark metrics and verifying the integrity and consistency of the deposited files. These scripts do not contain the restricted original project records or proprietary source-data processing materials. The archive is intended to support transparent audit and reproducibility of the released derived analyses while preserving the access restrictions applying to the underlying project data.
items.title: When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? — Project 06 Data and Reproducibility Package

items.summary: Self-contained computational materials accompanying "Verifiable approval-release decisions for construction project management: A provenance-aware contract and automated evidence" by Ahmad Baghdadi. Version 4.0.0 includes source code, complete generated inputs and results, schemas, exact witnesses, a de-identified calendar encoding, benchmark records and SHA-256 checksums. This version adds 83 conventional priority-list levelling comparisons under identical constraints: 72 tied peaks and 11 one-gate improvements, with sufficient exact certificates for all 83. A complete two-plan PROV-O example passes the domain and provenance SHACL profiles and preserves every decision field after RDF exchange. The suite comprises 145 automated tests. Earlier computational evidence includes generated extraction, 360 controlled record comparisons, exact wave bounds, nine calendar scenarios and 80 saved benchmark plans with renewed arithmetic audit. S14 preparation includes blank independent-annotation and approval registers plus a precision/recall evaluator with explicit denominators. No native baseline or independent annotations are available; field validation has not been executed. Case A remains historical aggregates only. Calendar B is a prior encoding with assumed review windows. Supplementary Table S1 identifies the deposited components and the supplement consolidates the evidence limits.
items.title: Reproducibility materials for verifiable approval-release decisions in construction project management

items.summary: This data and code release accompanies “Output rules and corpus preparation shape retrieval evaluation in a cross-language legal information audit”. Version 3.0 brings together the current rule experiment, internal task benchmark, legal-version evidence and selected research exports from the published version 2.1 baseline. The collection contains 39 Peruvian legal-information records. The output-rule component applies eight combinations of no-match handling, document-support filtering and tie ordering to frozen scores for 32 retained queries and 58 designated-target exposures per language path. It includes 6,912 query-level results, 216 aggregate summaries and a 5,000-replicate shared-order negative control. The internal benchmark contains twelve tasks in six clusters, two formulations per task, 468 provisional content grades, the two returned coding sets, four retrieval configurations and corpus-repair comparisons. Current sensitivity files evaluate existing grade sets, all 27 assignments to three unknown returned grades and RETA-family aggregation. Preparation and judgment roles, prior-output exposure and missing values are retained. Content support is evaluated separately from temporal applicability. The legal-evidence component supplies dated official-source locators, checksums and version findings. The archive includes current Figures 1–3, source data, plotting code, component data dictionaries, a result/file map, portable standard-library recalculation code and a SHA-256 manifest. Exported score/rank aggregation and deterministic sensitivity checks have been reproduced. Fresh extraction and scoring require the exact source carriers, indexed text and pinned model resources documented in the manifests. Original legal PDFs, full-text/OCR caches, source-page images and model weights are not redistributed. Project-created data and documentation retain the existing CC BY 4.0 licence; project-created code retains the MIT licence. Third-party source materials remain subject to their respective access and reuse conditions. The preceding published baseline is identified by DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23094356, and the version series by DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23094355.
items.title: CLIQ-R: Data and code for cross-language legal retrieval evaluation in Peru

items.summary: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.
items.title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation

items.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

items.summary: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
items.title: SceneAE: Scene Generation and Reconstruction in Queryable 3D-Anchored Latent Space

items.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.
items.title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23431625 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the research objectives. It states that the study aims to replicate the quantitative analysis of Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018), assess the reproducibility of their findings, and examine potential limitations concerning statistical power and model specification. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The replication approach is suitable for the research, as the authors reproduce the original Cox proportional hazards models and robustness tests. However, the methodological assessment has some gaps. In particular, the power analysis reports values of 0.44 and 0.99 without providing the formula, software procedure, or sufficient calculation details to allow readers to reproduce the estimates. The choice of 42 events in Table 6 also needs clarification, given that Table 5 reports 54 events overall. Additionally, the differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes remain unexplained. These issues weaken the transparency and reproducibility of the analysis. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The main conclusion is that the original findings can be reproduced, which is supported by the reported results. The authors also reasonably identify the small number of female-signatory agreements and the limitations of drawing causal conclusions from the observed association. However, the claim that the analysis has low statistical power relies on a calculation for which the formula and detailed procedure are not provided (Table 6). The differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes also remain unexplained. These limitations make some aspects of the interpretation less conclusive than they could be. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? Somewhat appropriate and clear The survival analysis and regression tables are suitable for presenting the findings. However, some numerical inconsistencies in the descriptive statistics and differences in sample sizes across the original and reproduced models need clarification to ensure the results are presented accurately. For instance, Table 3 presents: three major statistical flaws: 1: Conflict Intensity row, where Female Signatories = 1: has SD of 1.2 while the Max is 0.45, which is statistically incorrect. Similarly, (2) Democracy row where Female Signatories = 1, has Mean 0.92 < Min 1. And lastly, on page 5, UN peacekeeping is written as a binary number, however, in Table 3, the binary UN Peacekeeping has Max > 1. All these minor inconsistencies require clarification. How clearly do the authors discuss, explain, and interpret their findings and potential next steps for the research? Very clearly The authors explain their findings, acknowledge the limitations of the small number of agreements with female signatories, and discuss the implications for causal interpretation. They also identify the need for further research, although the power analysis and differences in sample sizes could be explained more transparently. Is the preprint likely to advance academic knowledge? Somewhat likely If the author clarified the sample-size discrepancies and documented the power analysis more transparently, then it would substantially contribute to the reproducibility of an influential finding, as it already highlights the reproducibility of the findings and highlights the limitations in statistical power and causal interpretation. Would it benefit from language editing? No The languages is clear and no major errors could be found hinderig the understanding of the resarch. However some minor issues could be corrected, such as, constant capitalisation of the first letter in column names. Would you
items.title: Structured PREreview of "Female Signatories and Peace Durability: Replicating Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018)"

items.summary: Learning intrinsic dynamics---the relationship between actions and their consequences---is essential for world models. However, visual variations unrelated to the underlying control process can obscure this relationship in learned representations. We investigate the connection between action predictability, defined as the ability to reconstruct an action from consecutive latent states, and the preservation of intrinsic dynamics. Our central hypothesis is that encouraging action predictability discourages representations from discarding the distinctions between different actions and their consequences. We provide two complementary forms of evidence for this connection. Theoretically, we derive a positive lower bound on squared inverse prediction error when the encoder merges distinguishable outcomes of different actions from the same state and appearance, and show that forward prediction can still be exact on those transitions. Empirically, controlled appearance-diversity comparisons, supervision interventions, and latent probes support the role of action prediction in preserving control-relevant transition information. We instantiate action predictability with Concat IDM, which predicts actions from concatenated latent states and updates the shared encoder using action labels already available in offline trajectories, without changing the test-time planner. Across three independent training runs on Push-T with 24 appearances, Concat IDM increases planning success from 9.1% to 77.2%; its paired improvement is 52.9 percentage points larger than that observed with a single appearance. Together, these findings support action predictability as an inductive bias toward intrinsic dynamics and demonstrate the practical benefits of Concat IDM for latent planning under visual diversity.
items.title: Learning Intrinsic Dynamics in Latent World Models

items.summary: This replication package contains the experimental artifacts, anonymized empirical benchmark dataset (N = 5,000 paired student-opportunity records), statistical verification scripts, database definitions, and microservices source code for the research paper: "Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement: An Empirical Study of Database-Level Vector Offloading" Targeted for Information and Software Technology (IST, Elsevier). Package Contents: data/: Anonymized benchmark dataset (students_data_tesis_final.csv) featuring 168-hour weekly availability matrices and raw ablation output. benchmarks/: Automated Python scripts for Stratified 5-fold cross-validation ablation (C1 to C4), Wilcoxon Signed-Rank hypothesis testing, Cliff's Delta effect size calculation, and bootstrap confidence intervals. database/: PostgreSQL 16 schema and stored procedure definitions for HNSW Approximate Nearest Neighbor vector search (pgvector) and dynamic schedule intersection. turborepo-src/: Clean source code of the decoupled microservices monorepo (API Gateway, Matching Service, ML Engine, and shared Protocol Buffers). System Requirements: Python 3.10+ with NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Scikit-Learn, and NLTK. Node.js v20+ / pnpm v9+ and Docker Engine for microservice orchestration.
items.title: Replication Package: Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement
